items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

ctx.x: And I started going around to different clubs; I went around to the Five Spot Firespot, and (unintelligible) and Jim Harlo, Hall, and who was there but Jimmy Giuffre, Jim and who was it that was on drums ... oh, the drummer, and Buell Neidlinger, Bill Nyad, a bassist that I knew; a white dude, that had been working mostly with Cecil Skeets Taylor. And they were good musicians.

And we were buddies. But I went in and I sat in with Giuffre for Dupree, and Giuffre Dupree wanted me to open up with him down at the Vanguard, and I didn't tell you this story, but back in the late fifties, '59, I hung strung out there in Harlem, and I come over to Brooklyn, and I had all my clothes and what not in this pawn shop, and I was going over there to get -- the guy knew me and all, I needed a few dollars, and I said, "Come on man, add some more on to the ticket, you know, and I'll come and get my…

get around, and that person wouldn't kill me until they got their fiddle, you know. It turned out later that it was Peck Morrison's bass. But however, naturally, we had to report it to the police, and that's when they started looking for me. That was before I went to Chicago, and I'm not thinking about that so much, because I knew he got his fiddle the next day; he got it back, but the police was still looking for me for petit petty larceny. And it didn't come to the floor until I got back there in '60, and I…
